content:
The first Home Ownership Scheme (HOS) building constructed using the Modular Integrated Construction (MiC) method, On Pak Court in Kwun Tong, has been occupied for only 15 months. Recently, owners have reported that the external wall paint is peeling, blistering, flaking off, and growing moss. The Collective (集誌社) visited the site on Thursday (the 8th) and observed that, although scaffolding workers were repainting at multiple locations and the bubbling was no longer visible on the external walls of On Pak Court, the neighbouring On Wah Court, also built using MiC, showed extensive bubbling on its external walls similar to On Pak Court, with multiple cracks on the estate's boundary wall and efflorescence seeping out. Some residents worry that problems will persist after the Housing Department's maintenance period expires, leaving owners to share the cost of repairs. They condemned the situation as "spending millions on a shoddy building" and hope the Housing Department will maintain the estate's common areas permanently.

On Pak Court and the neighbouring On Wah Court are the first HOS developments built by the Housing Department using the MiC construction method, in which residential units are prefabricated in Mainland factory facilities, with the structure, plumbing and electrical systems, and interior finishes completed before being transported to Hong Kong and assembled into the building.

On Wah Court external walls 'bubbling'

The Collective arrived at Anderson Road this afternoon for inspection. Repair work on the external walls of On Pak Court was found to be largely complete, although water seepage marks and cracks remained on the estate's boundary wall. However, the external walls of On Wah Court, also built using MiC and located just across the street, showed the same problems. On one facade, the entire 28-storey wall surface exhibited bubbling, with obvious unevenness at the joints between floors. The estate's boundary wall showed multiple long, narrow diagonal cracks with efflorescence seeping out, leaving white crystalline deposits on the surface. Mr and Mrs Cheung, residents of On Wah Court, said they had only moved in two months ago, with no leaks inside their unit, but they had noticed paint peeling and flaking off the orange-coloured sections of the external wall.

Recently, some On Pak Court owners reported to the media that many owners in the residents' group chat had been complaining about continuous water leaks since moving in. Some found water leaking in the kitchen and bathroom when taking possession of their units, and large areas of bubbling and flaking paint on the building's walls. Moss was growing from water leaking from external wall pipes, and some said cracks had appeared on the external walls of high floors, with the rubber sealing strips at the joints between modular units shrinking and splitting.

Toilet pipe leak discovered

Ms Wong, a resident of On Pak Court, took possession of her unit about half a year ago. She told The Collective that a leaking toilet pipe was found at the time, which the contractor repaired, and there had been no further leakage problems inside the unit since. However, she was unhappy that the new building was already peeling after only one year of occupation, and worried that more problems would arise after the maintenance period expired, asking: "What if the owners have to share the cost of major repairs?" Ms Wong hopes the Housing Department can "guarantee quality through to the end" and permanently handle the maintenance of common areas. She added that scaffolding workers had been carrying out repairs at the estate recently, with paint splattering onto her laundry, forcing her to dry her clothes indoors. She bluntly stated: "I spent millions buying a shoddy building."

Canopy cracks appeared shortly after

Another owner, Ms Tsang, moved in at the beginning of this year. Cracks appeared on the canopy not long after, and the contractor carried out repairs. It remains unknown whether cracks will reappear in "windy and rainy weather" in the future. She pointed out that fortunately, the owners were united enough to contact the District Council and the media for follow-up, which forced the Housing Department to carry out repairs. For now, she is not worried about having to bear high maintenance costs in the future.

On Wah Court was built by Shui On Construction, completed in August last year, with occupation beginning in November. On Wah Court provides 990 units across two blocks, ranging from 296 to 495 square feet, at an average price of HK$7,030 per square foot, with unit prices ranging from HK$1.81 million to HK$3.77 million. On Pak Court was part of the same contractor's project during the same period, with foundation work beginning in February 2022 and completion three years later. The single block offers 420 units with usable areas ranging from 291 to 498 square feet, at an average price of HK$7,000 per square foot, priced from HK$1.77 million to HK$3.73 million, with occupation starting in phases from July last year.

The Housing Department earlier replied to the media that after receiving complaints about On Pak Court in late July this year, it immediately urged the contractor to carry out comprehensive repairs. Following a drone survey, it was estimated that dust on certain areas of the external walls had not been thoroughly cleaned before painting, or that the primer had not been applied evenly, which was attributed to defective paintwork workmanship.

In addition, the department did not find any cracks in the wall structure, believing these were merely water stains on the external wall after rain. As for reports that "MiC module rubber seals had shrunk and split", the Housing Department confirmed after on-site verification and review of records that this was not the situation described by owners, but rather a workmanship defect caused by wall paint overflowing onto the rubber seals during application. Cleaning and repairs at those locations have been completed, and there is no leakage of any kind in the units.
